title: Your Blended Margin Looks Healthy. Some of What You Sell Is Quietly Losing Money.
linkedin:
Your gross margin percentage can sit in exactly the same band for six months while the business underneath it changes completely.

That is not a compliment to stability. It is usually an averaging effect.

A blended margin blends everything, every product, every service line, every customer segment. When one line loses margin and another gains it back by a similar amount, the total on the P&L barely moves. Nobody looks twice.

Here is the pattern we see most often once that number actually gets split apart by line. Growth has concentrated in the lower-margin part of the business, not the higher-margin part. A quiet-period offer that was priced to win the work, never repriced once things picked up. A newer customer segment that needs more hand-holding per dollar than the one the business was built on. A one-off discount that quietly became the standing rate for a whole category of work.

None of that shows up in the total. It shows up in a blended number that looks fine, sitting on top of two or three very different stories about what is actually making money.

The fix is not complicated once you see it. Break margin down by line, decide deliberately which ones you are scaling, fixing, repricing, or keeping on purpose as a loss leader, then keep checking often enough that drift gets caught early rather than discovered at year end.

Quick question for anyone who has actually split their margin by product or service line lately, not just looked at the total.

We see this pattern a lot. The overall gross margin looks steady, but underneath it one line has quietly gotten cheaper to run while another has quietly gotten more expensive, and the two cancel out on the page.

The line that is losing money is often the one that has been getting the most attention and the most new sales lately too, which is the annoying part.

Have you ever pulled your numbers apart by line and been surprised by what you found?

A note for East Coast business owners who keep half an eye on their gross margin percentage each month. If that number has stayed steady for a while, it is worth checking what is actually happening underneath it before assuming everything is fine.

A blended margin is an average across everything the business sells. When one product or service line loses margin and another gains a similar amount, the total on the page barely moves, even though the mix underneath has shifted. Growth tends to flow toward whatever is easiest to say yes to, and that is not always the most profitable part of the business.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses in Brisbane and across Queensland is usually the same. A quiet-period offer that was priced to win the work and never revisited. A newer type of customer that needs more time per dollar than the ones the business was built on. A one-off discount that became the standing rate without anyone deciding it should.

None of this shows up until the number gets split by line. Once it does, the picture is rarely subtle, and the decision about what to do with each line becomes a lot clearer.
